Learning Objectives
Review the potential etiologies that may contribute to coronal spine deformities.
Identify critical physical examination findings that may require additional workup in patients
with spinal deformity.
Apply the role and goals of plain radiography, MRI, and CT in the work up and surveillance of
coronal spine deformities.
Observe the historical contributions and advancements of several classification systems for
spinal deformity and how they provide clinical utility.
Identify patients with coronal spine deformities who may benefit from nonsurgical and surgical
treatment and determine modalities that provide the greatest effect.
Evaluate important factors in determining and predicting outcomes in patients with spinal
deformity.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Adult spine deformity (ASD) is a challenging spinal pathology and can be described as a
spectrum of disorders that occur in adults, including adult idiopathic or degenerative scoliosis,
sagittal and coronal malalignment, and iatrogenic deformity with or without concomitant
spinal stenosis.
The magnitude of coronal curvature is measured using the Cobb angle.
Definition of ASD
Coronal Cobb angle greater than 10° in a skeletally mature individual
Often three-dimensional, with deformities in the coronal, sagittal, and axial planes
Many studies have evaluated the effect of sagittal imbalance and malalignment; however, less
attention traditionally has been paid to coronal balance and alignment.
The prevalence of ASD may be higher than 50%; however, symptomatic ASD is lower than this
prevalence.
Symptoms
Individuals present with varying levels of back and leg pain.
Back pain is a common symptom.
May be diffuse or focally located near the apex of the main curve or the lumbosacral
fractional curve
Pain generators include degenerative disks and/or facets and muscle fatigue from worsening
alignment.
Back pain that is worse in an upright position and that improves in a supine position may be
a good prognostic sign for symptom relief after surgical management.
Leg pain
Leg pain may occur with varying degrees of severity and often depends on the location and
level of stenosis.
Commonly, patients experience radicular symptoms because of nerve compression at the
foramina or concavity of the coronal curve, especially at the lumbosacral fractional curve.
Traction radiculopathies can occur in patients with rotatory subluxations.
Central stenosis may result in neurogenic claudication.


Symptoms
ASD involves malalignment in the sagittal and coronal planes. Although sagittal
imbalance and malalignment have been well studied in literature, more attention
recently has been paid to the coronal alignment in patients with ASD. Adult scoliosis is
diagnosed in skeletally mature individuals with a coronal Cobb angle greater than 10°.1,2
This lesson focuses on the coronal deformities that may occur in the thoracic and
lumbar spine in patients with ASD.
ASD may be a cause back and leg pain for many patients. Back pain (more common) may
be caused by degenerative changes in the intervertebral disk and facets, and by muscle
fatigue from spinal imbalance; possibly exacerbated by rotational subluxation and
imbalance.3 More diffuse back pain with muscle fatigue may occur in patients with more
severe malalignment. Leg pain is a result of spinal stenosis and tension from rotary
subluxation, whereby foraminal stenosis may be more frequent than central stenosis.
Patients with central stenosis describe symptoms of neurogenic claudication, in which
pain or a sense of fatigue occur in their legs during walking.3 On stopping the activity
and resting, the pain is eliminated and walking can continue until the symptoms recur.
Epidemiology
The US population is aging, and aging is associated with an increase in the prevalence of
degenerative spinal deformities (8.3% to 68%).4
Kobayashi et al5 reported a 37% incidence of de novo development of degenerative scoliosis in
60 individuals aged 50 to 84 years over a period of 12 years.
Schwab et al6 evaluated 75 individuals with a mean age of 70.5 years who had no known
history of scoliosis or prior spine surgery. The authors determined that 68% of the individuals
had a Cobb angle greater than 10° (meeting the definition of scoliosis).
Based on Medicare data from 2001 to 2011, the number of spine fusions performed for the
management of ASD that involved seven or more levels increased 289% during that period.
The evaluation and management of ASD is an important area of focus because of an aging
population with increasing functional expectations.


Epidemiology
ASD is a growing healthcare concern, especially in the aging population, because studies
have shown a prevalence as high as 60% in the elderly population. The overall
prevalence of ASD in the literature ranges from 8.3% to 68%.4 Given the inherent
relationship between age and the progression of degenerative spine deformities,5 ASD is
one of the most frequent indications for surgical treatment among patients older than
65 years.6 Therefore, ASD remains an important area of focus because of an aging
population with increasing functional expectations. The incidence of spinal surgery for
adult degenerative spinal deformities also is increasing because the reported outcomes
of older patients are equivalent to those of younger patients, given adjustments for
associated medical conditions.7 Although the incidence of spinal degenerative disease
and treatment options from individual centers or small cohort analyses have been noted
in the past, a paucity of data is available on the incidence of spinal surgery for the
management of ASD from a population standpoint in the United States; however, large
Medicare databases reveal considerable increases in surgical treatment for patients with
ASD.8
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The thoracic spine has 12 mobile segments: T1 through T12. T1 through T10 each have a pair
of ribs that are joined anteriorly at the costochondral junction or sternum.
The lumbar spine typically has five mobile segments—L1 through L5—except in individuals
with lumbarization or sacralization of the transitional vertebra.
Coronal Cobb measures greater than 10° define scoliosis.
Curvatures may be defined as structural or compensatory.
Nerves
Commonly, patients experience radicular symptoms because of nerve compression at the
foramina or concavity of the coronal curve, especially at the lumbosacral fractional curve.

Musculature
The paraspinal musculature and psoas are important for maintenance of postural balance.
The influence of frailty and sarcopenia spine deformity has garnered much attention in
relation to vertebral fragility fractures, spinal malalignment, and surgical outcomes.
Multifidus muscle cross-sectional area is smaller and fatty infiltration higher in the multifidus
and longissimus muscles, considerably on the concave side of the curve at all levels in patients
with coronal deformity.
Multifidus and erector muscles aid in maintenance of pelvic alignment. In addition, paraspinal
muscles (multifidus and erector spinae) are associated with the pathology of ASD (based on
MRI) compared with appendicular muscle evaluations using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry
(DEXA).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
A clear and detailed understanding of normal spinal anatomy is important in
understanding possible pathologic entities in patients with spinal deformity. The spine
consists of four distinct regions: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacropelvic. Specifically,
the thoracic spine consists of 12 mobile segments, many of which are connected to ribs
(T1 through T10). T11 and T12 usually have floating ribs that are not connected anteriorly
to the rib cage. In the lumbar spine, five mobile segments are present. The sacropelvic
unit consists of five fused segments of the sacrum that articulate with the ilium through
the sacroiliac joints bilaterally and the coccyx. As measured by the Cobb angle, coronal
curvatures may be defined as compensatory or structural. Structural curves often are
rigid and the largest is the major curve. Compensatory curves present in response to a
structural curve as the body attempts to maintain coronal alignment. These
compensatory minor curves generally appear smaller and flexible on dynamic plain
radiographs.
The exiting nerve root often may be compressed at the concavity of the coronal
curvature. In the degenerative setting, this is especially common in the region of the
fractional curve. This is important because the compression often may be relieved via
correction of the coronal curvature.

The muscular system plays an essential role in the maintenance of postural balance. The
paraspinal and psoas muscles involved in pelvic positioning and lumbar stabilization are
at the forefront of new research.9 Aging and concomitant sarcopenia can affect the
radiographic and clinical progression related to coronal deformities.10 The effects of
paraspinal muscles on coronal and sagittal spinopelvic parameters in patients with ASD
have been reported.11
Etiology
Primary degenerative scoliosis (de novo scoliosis)
Curve location: thoracolumbar or lumbar spine with the apex generally located at L2-3 or L3-
4
Etiology: facet joint degeneration/arthrosis and disk degeneration in an asymmetric manner
Progressive idiopathic scoliosis
Curve location: follows the patterns commonly observed in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
Etiology: often, history of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis that progresses throughout
adulthood because of degeneration or mechanical factors
Secondary adult scoliosis
Curve location: thoracolumbar or lumbosacral
Etiology: pelvic obliquity, transitional anatomy (in the lumbosacral region), an adjacent
thoracolumbar or thoracic curvature of various origins (idiopathic, neuromuscular, or
congenital)
Secondary scoliosis
Curve location: varies throughout entire spine
Etiology: osteoporosis or metabolic bone disease

Etiology
Primary etiologies of coronal deformities in the thoracic and/or lumbar spine can be
divided into progression of adolescent scoliosis or degenerative/de novo scoliosis.3 A
coronal deformity also may occur secondary to other various anatomic variants
(adjacent coronal curves, transitional anatomy pelvic obliquity) or medical conditions

(osteoporosis, metabolic bone disease). Coronal curvatures in the degenerative setting
generally are of less magnitude than those observed in adolescent idiopathic curves. The
prevalence of coronal deformities in residual adolescent scoliosis and degenerative
scoliosis are approximately 6% in adults older than 50 years.12 The degenerative cascade
is launched after the predicted loss of disk hydration and disk space height, with
subsequent increased loads on the facets that cause facet degeneration. The
degeneration of these elements may cause instability in the spinal column and lead to
scoliosis.
Natural History
Most adolescent idiopathic scoliosis curves progress at a rate of less than 1° per year;
thoracolumbar curves progress at a mean of approximately 0.5° per year, and lumbar curves
progress at a mean of approximately 0.24° per year.
Coronal thoracic curves less than 30° tend not to progress.
Ascani et al13 reported on 187 patients followed for more than15 years after skeletal maturity;
20° to 29° coronal curves progressed a mean of 10°, 30° to 39° coronal curves progressed a
mean of 12°, 40° to 49° coronal curves progressed a mean of 15°, and 50° to 59° coronal
curves progressed a mean of 20°.
If pulmonary function at skeletal maturity is normal, progression of adult degenerative coronal
deformities does not usually lead to a decline in pulmonary function.

Natural History
In general, as curve size increases, the likelihood of progression increases,14 possibly
because of the influence of gravity and the increasing imbalance that results from larger
curves. In patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, more curves greater than 30°
progress approximately less than 1° per year;15 however, several studies following
patients for the long term have described that curves greater than 80° to 90° do not
progress or progress at a much slower rate than smaller curves.15 Although no widely
accepted theory exists with regard to this progression in the more severe coronal curves,
possible explanations include the rigidity that results from degenerative changes, the

spontaneous fusion that has been observed at the apex of severe curves, and the
stability provided by the rib cage resting on the pelvis.16
Given the decreased pulmonary function that may be observed in patients with severe
forms of adolescent coronal deformities, progressive coronal deformity in adult
degenerative presentations theoretically may lead to a deterioration of pulmonary
function; however, no evidence that suggests that an adult patient with previously
normal pulmonary function (after skeletal maturity) will experience pulmonary function
deterioration because of progression of the curvature without a history of smoking or
other pulmonary diseases.
Dissimilar from the array of coronal curve presentations in adult idiopathic scoliosis,
coronal deformity in the degenerative scoliosis curve typically occurs in the lumbar
spine. As patients age and develop additional degeneration of the vertebrae and
surrounding structures, curves may progress at a faster rate.17 Curvatures of less than
20° are less likely to progress than more severe curves because the mechanical loads
that are produced may be below the threshold required to induce cellular changes
leading to degenerative spine changes.
Risk Factors
The onset of coronal deformity in scoliosis is associated with multiple theories, including
possible relationships with posture, balance, muscle structure, psychology, height, vision,
hearing, hormones, birth injury, and genetics.
For most coronal deformities in patients of all ages, initial cause and effect remain relatively
unclear, partly because a deformed spine has potential to induce diverse secondary changes
by virtue of its comprehensive role in human biology.

Risk Factors
Numerous hypotheses have been presented with regard to the manner in which coronal
deformities occur in certain individuals (Table 1). Recently, a great deal of research has

described the molecular and cellular changes that occur within various aspects of spinal
anatomy as coronal deformity occurs. Although the initial trigger that commences
coronal spine curvature remains relatively unknown, a large body of research has
demonstrated that asymmetric loading of the spine results in biomechanical forces that
may account for most, if not all, progression of the spinal deformity. A summary of
current data suggests that a threshold for continuous asymmetric loading exists and
must be reached before coronal changes occur in the vertebrae and that transient
loading likely will not foster the asymmetric growth that progresses to deformity.

Classification
Aebi2 proposed a classification system based on the etiology of the curve, designed to focus
primarily on the natural history of the deformity; however, but this classification system did
not guide the surgical management of ASD.
Schwab et al18 proposed a classification system for adult scoliosis that included a system of
graded clinical parameters (apex, lumbar lordosis, and intervertebral subluxation).
The Scoliosis Research Society (SRS) proposed a classification system for ASD based on
radiographic parameters, using concepts from the King-Moe and the Lenke classification
systems.19
Kuntz et al20 created a classification system for spinal deformity based on age-dependent
neutral upright spinal alignment; spinal abnormality; deformity curve location, pattern,
magnitude, and flexibility; and global spinal alignment.
The SRS-Schwab Adult Spinal Deformity Classification was subsequently developed to
incorporate the Schwab classification system based on health-related quality of life (HRQOL)
measures and radiographic outcomes, including pelvic parameters.21
Obeid et al22 recently proposed a classification system focused on coronal spinopelvic
malalignment, consisting of treatment algorithms based on convex or concave presentations.

Classification
Most classification systems describing spinal deformity were designed to describe
pediatric spinal deformities. One of the earliest ASD classification systems that
accounted for coronal plane changes was proposed in 2001 by Simmons.23 Two types of
deformities were describe, one of which is degenerative lumbar scoliosis with no or
minimal rotational deformity (type I) and the other of which is degenerative scoliosis
often superimposed on preexisting scoliosis with greater rotational deformity and
greater loss of lordosis (type II). In 2005, Aebi2 classified ASD in three types based on
etiology (Table 2). This classification system primarily was designed to correlate with the
natural history of the deformity but could not determine patients who would benefit
from surgical treatment. In the same year, Schwab et al24 proposed a radiographic
classification system based on lordosis from L1 through S1 and coronal plane obliquity
of L3 observed on standing radiographs (Table 3). To improve on this classification
system, the next year, Schwab et al18 proposed a new classification system based on the
previously established “high impact clinically significant radiographic parameters” via a
prospective study of 947 patients with ASD. In 2007, this classification system was
modified to account for patients with deformity in the sagittal plane alone, with the
addition of a sixth group and a global balance modifier25 (Table 4).

Patient History
A complete patient history followed by a careful physical examination are essential. The
clinical presentation of a coronal spine deformity may vary widely, from no symptoms to
severe pain with disability. A large percentage of patients may remain asymptomatic,
with only radiographic findings of scoliosis noted.25 Assessment of an adult with a
coronal spine deformity should be no different from the evaluation of any patient with
back pain or spine pathology. Although new or progressive back pain is the most
common presentation, degenerative changes in the lumbosacral spine may result in
varying amounts of back and/or leg pain. Patients may describe a history of diffuse back
pain and muscle fatigue if presenting with substantial coronal (and/or sagittal) imbalance
(Figure 1). The intensity of the pain and related disability caused by leg and back pain
must be quantified. Information about alleviating and aggravating factors also should be
elicited. The timing of spine deformity diagnosis (adolescence versus adulthood) and
whether the patient has a history of spine infection, tumor, or traumatic injury should be
determined (Table 9).

A full panel of sensory testing will differentiate spinal root pathology (dermatomal

Normal coronal alignment usually refers to a thoracic and lumbar curve without
substantial curvature. A coronal deformity is present if a Cobb angle of more than 10°
can be measured on PA or AP standing radiographs. The Cobb angle is the maximal
curve of a particular region of the spine formed by the most angled superior vertebra
and the most angled lower vertebra. Parallel lines to the superior and inferior end plates
are used to measure the Cobb angle. The upper-end vertebra and the lower-end
vertebra are the proximal and distal vertebrae composing a structural curve. Specifically,
the end vertebra is the most tilted vertebra in the horizontal plane. The defined curve
location depends on the location of the apical vertebra, which is the vertebra that is the
most considerably displaced from the midline, the most horizontal, and the most
rotated. The neutral vertebra is the vertebra that has the least rotation distal to the main
structural curve as observed on a coronal radiograph. The stable vertebra usually is the
most cephalad vertebra directly distal to the major curve that is most closely bisected by
the central sacral vertical line (CSVL). Historically, Nash and Moe29 proposed a method to
measure vertebral rotation on plain radiographs. The authors divided the vertebral body
into six equivalent sections with three sections on each side of the spinous process in a
non-rotated vertebra (neutral). With increasing rotation, the pedicle on the concave side
moves toward the edge of the vertebral body, whereas the convex pedicle moves toward
the midline.
The CSVL is a vertical line drawn from the center of S1, which helps determine coronal
balance. Similarly, the C7 plumb line (C7PL) is drawn straight down from the middle of
the C7 vertebral body (Figure 4). Apical vertebral translation can be identified by locating
the apex of a curve and measuring the distance from the centroid to the CSVL or C7PL.
Therefore, the horizontal distance between these two lines is the coronal vertical axis or

Deformity Correction
Correction of coronal spine deformity via rod placement often is the most technically
challenging aspect of surgical management of scoliosis. It requires a thorough
understanding of the three-dimensional forces required to improve spinal alignment and
create a construct that is stable to aid in spinal fusion.
Rod derotation is a commonly used technique for the reduction of coronal curvatures. In
theory, the technique is simple and effective at rotating a scoliotic helix toward the
sagittal plane. The amount of derotation at individual vertebrae in the axial plane may be
limited in a pure rod rotation correction maneuver; however, this is disputed by some
who suggest that considerable apical vertebral rotation occurs in posterior derotation
maneuvers and in the overall correction of a coronal deformity into the sagittal plane.41
Rod derotation often is described via the posterior approach but also may be performed
via open anterior and thoracoscopic approaches. For segmental derotation, after
placement of pedicle screws at planned levels, the concave rod is placed initially as
usual. The surgeon should identify the proximal and distal neutral vertebrae and secure
them with the use of derotation devices to act as a counterforce for the rotatory
maneuvers (Figure 8). Then, rod derotation and translation are applied to reduce the
rod into the screw tulips. The convex derotation device should be forced downward and
medially as the concave device is forced upward by a pulling vector. Concurrently, the
neutral vertebrae should be forced toward the contralateral side, and more downward
force can be applied across the rib hump (if present).42 For en bloc derotation, the
derotation devices are attached to all intervening levels. The entire segment can connect
through a locking device and, therefore, provide simultaneous rotation of the entire
segment.

Minimally invasive surgery techniques for spine deformity correction have improved in

invasive surgical techniques must be able to achieve the same goals as an open

widely accepted in describing coronal deformities in the lumbar spine.50 In addition,
minimally invasive surgical techniques should not be performed in patients with rigid
deformities (in the setting of fused segments) and patients with osteoporosis.

increase the accuracy of the procedure and instrumentation placement by virtually

Outcomes
If coronal and sagittal balance is achieved and maintained via solid fusion, outcomes generally
are good.
HRQOL improves more with surgical management than with nonsurgical management.
Pulmonary improvement after surgical correction is unlikely to occur in the adult population.
Despite these relatively modest gains, patient satisfaction generally is high (as high as 90%).
Correction of L4 and L5 coronal tilt may be predictive of the ability to correct and maintain
coronal deformity correction.
Osteoporosis, the anterior component of surgical management, and prior spine surgery are
factors associated with decompensation of coronal correction over time.

Outcomes
Surgical management of ASD often is associated with HRQOL improvement. In most
patients, the goal of coronal correction is spinal balance rather than coronal balance,
and Cobb angle correction is not necessary. Pulmonary improvement after surgical
correction is unlikely to occur in the adult population. Thoracoplasty may decrease
pulmonary function. Correction of coronal curvature often varies from 30° to 60°, and
ultimately is dependent on the nature of the preoperative coronal curve, flexibility, and
the technique used for coronal correction. Despite these relatively modest gains, patient
satisfaction generally high (as high as 90%).
The natural history of coronal alignment after surgical correction has been an area of
recent study. Osteoporosis, the anterior component of surgical management, and a
history of surgery before the deformity correction all contribute to decompensation of
coronal balance over time.61 The ability maintain coronal plane correction has been
attributed to the ability to level the coronal tilt of L4 and L5.62 A clear interplay exists
between coronal and sagittal deformity correction and patient outcomes. Daubs et al63
specifically evaluated the importance of coronal balance on spinal deformity outcomes.
